title: Let memory be sweet
hookLine: let the memory of lost friends become pleasant, like old fruit (Letters 63)

cards: There's a moment, a while after someone dies, when their name comes up at dinner and, for the first time, people laugh.
Somebody tells the story about the burnt turkey or the terrible car, and the laugh is real, and nobody feels guilty. The loss isn't smaller. The memory has changed flavor.
The same sixty-third letter that holds Seneca's confession also holds the hope for this moment, borrowed from one of his own teachers, with an image from the kitchen and the cellar.

teach.b: Let us see to it, Seneca says, that the memory of those we've lost becomes a pleasure: not a wound we keep pressing, but something we're glad to return to.
Then he quotes Attalus, the Stoic who taught him when he was young.
The memory of dead friends, Attalus used to say, is like certain fruits that are pleasantly sharp, or like very old wine, where the bitterness itself delights us. At first the taste is mostly sting.
With time, the sting becomes part of what makes it rich. Seneca adds a shift in grammar.
Instead of I have lost them, think: I have had them. The friendship happened. It was real.
Nothing that comes later can undo the years you were given. And a warning.
Because nobody knows how long they'll keep anyone, let's enjoy our friends greedily while we have them. Think how often we've left them for some trip, some work, some trivial errand.
The sweet memory starts now, in the time still shared. This path met a cousin of this on day four hundred twenty-three: figs in season.
Attalus's version is the cellar, where time turns bitter into something you'd pour for a guest.

how: Some people mark the memory of those they've lost by telling happy stories about them, and readers of Seneca sometimes use his phrase 'I have had them' when they remember.

o: a memory so painful it's best left well alone
a pleasant memory, like sharp fruit or very old wine
a toast Romans drank at a friend's funeral feast

p: not only I have lost them

s: Seneca says the memory of the dead should always stay painful
he hopes it becomes a pleasure, like sharp fruit or old wine.
the fruit and wine image comes from Seneca's teacher Attalus
Seneca quotes him in the sixty-third letter.
Seneca says to enjoy friends greedily while we have them
nobody knows how long they'll keep anyone.

games.q: a year after a friend dies, you laugh at a story about them and feel guilty. what would Seneca's letter say?
o: this is the memory turning sweet, as it should.
games.why: Seneca, quoting Attalus, hopes memory becomes pleasant, like old wine whose bitterness delights.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone simply far away now, and let one specific, sweet memory come: a joke, a meal, the way they said your name.
Notice the sting if there is one, and the sweetness underneath, both together, like that sharp fruit. Then, inside, try the words: I had you.

wordCard.voice: Iucunda memoria. Attalus's image, in Seneca's letter: remembering lost friends can become like sharp fruit or old wine, where the bitterness delights. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a pleasant memory, Seneca's hope for how we remember the dead (Letters 63.4–5).

carryVoice: Your line: sweet memory. I have had them, and that can't be undone. Until tomorrow.
